RESPONSE:
# Points from "How We Work", from memory

**Introduction**
1. The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
2. It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
3. This applies to claims from any source: papers, colleagues, summaries, your own earlier notes.
4. A claim's weight comes partly from the evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
5. Ask of each claim who has examined it and how closely.
6. Conclusions from colleagues with years in an area have usually been tested in ways not visible on the page.
7. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they've already made.
8. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
9. Overstating and understating are both costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little and undermine confidence in good work.
10. Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2. Take in what was said before you answer**
11. Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This keeps a conversation moving rather than circling; it isn't just politeness.
12. Start from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
13. Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
14. If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
15. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step.
16. Example: a manager sends a five-point request with a budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, pick up what you can act on now, and say the budget will follow in due course.

**§3. Go to the source**
17. Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to go back to primary material every time.
18. A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
19. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
20. Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
21. A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into private versions of the truth and stops being able to act.
22. Example: before citing a team note that a report showed "costs fell 12%" in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4. Do not leave open what can be closed**
23. Mark which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves uncertain, then keep the work moving.
24. Open questions block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
25. When the evidence leans clearly one way, record that as the working answer. It can be revisited later; a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
26. The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safer, is the more common one in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
27. When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save energy for live questions.
28. Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5. Help the colleague who sees differently**
29. New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see material differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful; a reviewer starting from scratch mostly rediscovers what the team knows.
30. When asking for a check, give context: what you've concluded, where you see the risks, what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
31. In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
32. Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right. Don't raise a half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement; take it to the person afterwards once you're sure.

**§6. Make your moves where they will land well**
33. Before taking a step, check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind: share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, release when ready.
34. Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be redone with colleagues, costing more than a short conversation would have.
35. The owner can see considerations you can't; asking first is how you learn them.
36. This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps don't need sign-off, but for steps that affect others the default is to check first and then act together.
37. Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether they'd like it restructured, and how.

**§7. Failures come in pairs**
38. Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other.
39. The pairs:
   - overclaiming / second-guessing;
   - inventing a flaw / overlooking one;
   - closing too early / keeping open too long;
   - abandoning a line / relitigating one;
   - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively;
   - acting alone / waiting too long.
40. If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
41. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
42. It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step; it describes careful work going well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
43. What keeps it honest is the team: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, an agreed direction. "Trust those."
